data.title: Nižná Myšľa – a Bronze Age town in eastern Slovakia
data.excerpt: On the Várhegy rise above the confluence of the Hornád, the Olšava and the Torysa, the people of the Otomani culture built an important fortified settlement in eastern Slovakia. Two overlapping hillforts stood here for roughly 300 years; the second of them gained almost 7 ha and became a centre of bronze casting and of power. Its cemetery, with an estimated 700 graves, is one of the most extensive in the Carpathian Basin.

children.text: Nižná Myšľa is an eastern Slovak village on the boundary between the Košice Basin, the foot of the Slanské vrchy hills and the confluence of the rivers Hornád, Olšava and Torysa. It differs markedly from other similar villages, however, in its exceptionally rich Bronze Age history, when the people of the Otomani culture built an important hillfort in the area of Nižná Myšľa. The hillfort was situated on the prominent rise of Várhegy above the confluence of the rivers mentioned, a strategically advantageous position at an elevation of 217 metres. Year after year archaeologists bring new and interesting discoveries from there.

In eastern Slovakia, in the setting of the Otomani–Füzesabony culture (approximately 1700 to 1400 BC), fortified settlements or hillforts of craftsmen and farmers came into being. Besides Nižná Myšľa, the best known is the hillfort of Spišský Štvrtok, which many people also call the Slovak Mycenae. The hillforts of the people of the Otomani culture (it is assumed that these people came to the territory of present-day Slovakia from the area of Transylvania) became not only centres of production, but also social and administrative centres of power which stamped the development of the time with the character of an advanced civilisation. Settlements with massive fortifications and a planned layout of their enclosures, cult places, cemeteries and the monuments of material and spiritual culture are eloquent testimony to the level of that age and are evidence of the creative abilities, skill and artistic sensibility of the ancient inhabitants of eastern Slovakia.

children.text: Research so far indicates that we are dealing with two mutually overlapping hillforts of the Otomani culture period. The fortified settlement existed there for roughly 300 years. In the period to which we assign it, several upheavals occurred in Eurasia, the consequence of which was a marked movement of population. It is sometimes also called the first migration of peoples. Specifically, these were the conflicts of the Hyksos in Egypt and the overthrow of the Hittite Empire, of Mycenae and of Crete. The whole of Europe, from the south as far as the British Isles, was gripped by armed conflicts and by the migration of fleeing or invading populations. It was precisely in this period that life existed in this settlement, and for that reason the settlement at Nižná Myšľa is fortified.

The hillfort lay at the crossing of several trade routes. For that reason its people were in contact with other, wealthier cultures, but also with peoples who threatened them. From the south these were the Mediterranean cultures and the Hittite Empire, and from the north the cultures around the Baltic Sea. Since the settlement at Nižná Myšľa lay directly on the route of the Amber Road, moreover at a place where it crossed other routes, it could be expected that its people had amassed a quantity of property. Among other things, there is evidence that the inhabitants of the local settlements were important traders in metal products, which at that time was one of the most lucrative lines of goods.

The conditions for the emergence and rapid rise of the fortified settlements in eastern Slovakia were undoubtedly also influenced by the rapid development of the metallurgy of non-ferrous metals. The prospecting for and processing of copper ore from local deposits, and later also the production of bronze objects, influenced the development of the basic branches of production existing until then and sharply accelerated the social development of the Bronze Age population.
Hillfort I

The oldest settlement (fortified settlement I) arose on the southern edge of the rise, and its fortification linked the steep drops of the promontory in an arc. The fortification consisted of a massive earthen rampart and a pointed ditch six metres deep, which was altered and widened twice. The protected enclosure of the settlement, with an area of 50 × 60 metres, was built up by its inhabitants with rectangular single-roomed houses. These were grouped in two rows separated by a street and followed the line of the fortification in parallel. The houses, with clay floors, were probably of log type with stone footings and hearths. Besides rich pottery vessels, the inventory consisted of stone grinders and grinding slabs, mauls and hoes, objects of bronze and bone, and clay loom weights and spindle whorls. These finds point to the agricultural and craft character of the occupation and attest to the local processing of primary and secondary raw materials. Among the remarkable pottery finds are clay figures of animals, small figurines of women and a hoard of small jugs hidden beneath the floor of one of the dwellings. The twofold rebuilding of the fortification system of settlement I that has been identified attests to its longer, probably uninterrupted occupation. During the last rebuilding of the fortification, which chronologically already falls at the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age, not only was the most massive ditch, up to 20 metres wide, dug, but the older, evidently already destroyed earthen rampart was also renewed, and the inhabitants of the settlement reinforced its new front wall with a further 1 metre thick layer of loess.

children.text: The youngest settlement horizon was almost completely destroyed by intensive ploughing. Its former existence is indicated today only by sunken domestic features which cut the older settlement layer and the dwellings. Similar sunken features, clay pits, storage and refuse pits were identified and uncovered in the approach area of the fortified settlement. The subsequent demise of the youngest ditch, in the fill of which finds of fragments of human bones were also strikingly frequent, probably did not mean a break in the continuity of occupation of the site. The further, subsequent occupation of the site was connected with the emergence of a new, more extensive fortified settlement II, when both the original area of settlement I and the area of the cemetery were included in the new enclosure.
Hillfort II

Through new, extensive building activity, which at the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age was probably forced on the settlement by its growing population or by new incomers (but evidently also by the threat of military attacks by an unknown enemy), the original enclosure of the settlement was enlarged sevenfold. By digging a new ditch and building a new arc-shaped rampart, this time with a stone-earth-and-timber construction, they gained almost 7 ha of fortified area, and at that point all the previous settlement forms and the cemetery lost their original significance and gradually ceased to exist. The enclosure of the new, exceptionally extensive settlement II was built up with large dwellings, again of log type, to which numerous sunken domestic features belonged. Traces of the later occupation were recorded both in the area of the original settlement I and in its partly filled ditch, and also above the older graves. The new, massive and technically more perfect line of fortification also had an arc-shaped ground plan, and it seems that a substantial part of the houses was again built in a double row, hugging the inner face of the rampart. Unfortunately, because these dwellings were originally of ground-level type, they were largely devastated by the subsequent intensive ploughing that lasted for centuries. Of the houses only the scattered remains of their stone footings survive, together with the stones that strengthened their post-built construction.

At this time bronze casting became one of the decisive craft activities in the settlement, and that evidently secured the expansion and prosperity of this centre. Besides dozens of stone moulds for casting bronze products, bronze casting lumps, bronze objects intended for remelting, misfired pieces and finished objects were also found in the refuse pits. A unique find, the torso of a casting mould, also attests to the local production of cast gold jewellery at the site.

Fortified settlement II was exceptional not only for its extraordinarily large extent and hence for the concentration of population, but also, as the recorded remains of the stone facing of the rampart show, it was an important centre of power. In eastern Slovakia contemporary stone walls have been found only at the site near Spišský Štvrtok. As there, the cemetery at Nižná Myšľa was also a centre of cult.
The demise of the hillfort

After years of prosperity and flowering, the inhabitants of the hillfort also lived through very hard times. The most serious situation must have arisen around 1500 BC. It is precisely the strengthening of the fortification within hillfort II and the increase in the number of inhabitants that may suggest that the inhabitants expected that they could be attacked by an enemy with a large military force, against which it was necessary to prepare appropriately. In the end, however, not even the strengthening and enlargement of the hillfort saved the inhabitants from catastrophe. At the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age the hillfort was destroyed by a massive fire.

There is nothing to suggest that anyone ever returned to the settlement. On its site archaeologists uncovered only the black burnt debris of houses and objects. No remains of buildings of later periods were found there. It is an interesting phenomenon. At Ždaňa there is evidence from the Early Iron Age and the Late Bronze Age. In the surrounding area there is also evidence attesting to the presence of people of the Celtic period, of the arrival of the Germanic peoples, the Slavs and the Avars, and of the Middle Ages. All of this was in the immediate neighbourhood, but the place where the Myšľa settlement had stood remained deserted. As if it were some kind of taboo. It is really interesting all the more because it stands in an advantageous location.
Religious cult

Among other things, a developed religious cult is attested by the find spots of sacrificial pits in which parts of people, or whole people, were ritually thrown. The bloody cult rites, in which besides animal and other common offerings human sacrifice was also exceptionally practised, were surely motivated by fear of danger, of crop failure or perhaps of disease. They were discovered not only in the surrounding area but also in Nižná Myšľa itself. Human offerings were thrown into them for the deities of the underworld. The most recently found sacrificial pit is to be exhibited in the local archaeological museum. Four bodies of young girls were found in it. According to anatomical features they were still virgins. Their arms were crossed and tied on their chests. They lay in the same position, face down on their stomachs.

Excavation established that they had been thrown into the pit at short intervals of time, approximately around 1450–1500 BC, when the settlement came to an end. From this it can be deduced that these were sacred offerings made just before a battle, and that their purpose was to win the deities over to the side of the inhabitants of the settlement. Various sacrificial objects were found with the offerings, such as food, ears of grain and gifts, but also, for example, the boiled skull of a child of about five years. It was therefore certainly a serious situation. The offerings, however, evidently did not help the inhabitants of the settlement. Archaeologists discovered only burnt ruins and signs which show that burning the settlement down was not the worst thing the conquerors did to them.

In one of the refuse pits gold and bronze jewellery was found. This is evidence that this culture was able to produce jewellery from gold, and it is interesting that the jewellery was hidden in a refuse pit, which shows that this was a desperate flight of the population at a time when they were attacked by conquerors. In their flight they had to hide their valuables in a place where the intruders would not find them. The fact that they did not come back for the jewellery suggests that they were probably killed, or else carried off into slavery.
The cemetery and its secrets

The cemetery at Nižná Myšľa is one of the most extensive contemporary necropolises known from the Carpathian Basin. We assume that the total number of graves may have been around 700. The oldest graves were dug by the western slope of the rise, and the cemetery gradually extended eastwards. Burial took place in more or less continuous rows, and separate small groups, nests of graves, were also identified.

The continuous burial of the dead over approximately 200 years in seven more or less continuous rows probably reflects the kinship, traditional extended-family relationships of successive generations. The three isolated groups of graves uncovered so far, with between 8 and 10 individuals, belong according to their grave goods to the youngest horizon of the cemetery and perhaps represent smaller independent families. These nests of graves have so far been identified only on the northern edge of the cemetery, and their grave inventory is poorer in comparison with the graves from the core of the cemetery. In the nests of graves there appeared in every case only one grave of an adult man and 2 to 4 graves of women, the rest being graves of children. These separate groups of graves belonged to contemporaries living outside the fortified settlement. Allowing their dead to be buried in the common cemetery, but in isolation, perhaps attests to the relations of the inhabitants of the fortified settlement towards the surrounding, evidently poorer and probably also subordinate population.

children.text: The results of the excavation of the cemetery have shown that the society of the time was already socially and economically differentiated. This is attested by the differences identified in the treatment of the grave pits, by the occasional use of various wooden burial containers and by the number and quality of the accompanying funerary inventory. As a rule the graves of adult, wealthy and important individuals were larger and about two metres deep. It was precisely in the graves of warriors, hunters and craftsmen that traces of combined timber reinforcement of the pits, or the remains of wooden coffins, were often found.

The archaeological excavation of the cemetery demonstrates that the inhabitants of the settlement believed in an afterlife. The stereotyped position of the dead in a crouched position determined the recurring arrangement of their grave inventory. The placing of objects of personal equipment as a rule followed from their previous practical purpose. Varied jewellery of bronze, gold, amber, shell, faience, bone, antler and ivory formed part of the dressing of the hair, the bodies, the clothing and the funeral robes. Weapons were placed by the hands, or where they were commonly worn. This applies especially to quivers with arrows behind the back and daggers with stone whetstones behind the belt. Working tools, blanks and working aids were most often placed at the feet of the dead. Pottery, in which there was food and drink intended for the afterlife, was placed by the lower limbs, more rarely in the lap, or by the head, right in front of the mouth or behind the skull. In graves with a timber construction a vessel placed on the lid of the coffin occasionally occurred. The number of vessels in the individual graves ranged between 1 and 8 examples. The pottery was made specially for funerary purposes; only rarely was a utilitarian settlement vessel used as a grave offering. The funerary pottery was as a rule poorly fired, but in comparison with the finds from the settlement it was considerably more decorative. The variability of the funerary pottery is also markedly smaller and is in principle limited to the predominant use of bowls, jugs, pots, cups and their miniature imitations. A unique find is the clay model of a cart from child's grave no. 40, which may originally have had a cult significance as well.

blocks.alt: Nižná Myšľa - a town of the Bronze Age

children.text: Perhaps fear of the dead, but also other reasons, sometimes led the survivors to reopen graves and subsequently to disturb the bodily remains of the dead. In such cases either the individual parts of the body were deliberately separated, the lower limbs were removed, or the chest area was weighed down with a boulder. The reason for the operations mentioned was probably a belief in the existence of vampires; the secondary interventions on the buried individuals probably had a protective purpose. Almost 30 per cent of the graves were evidently disturbed by secondary interventions, which were apparently carried out shortly after they had been filled in. These interventions are attested by funnel-shaped shafts, most often driven into the area of the head and chest of the buried people. Whether this was robbing in the true sense of the word, or the ritual removal of the most valuable grave offerings from the graves, can hardly be determined today. The focus of attention was certainly gold jewellery, insignia of power and massive weapons of bronze, which was very valuable at that time. Grave robbing, identified practically in all contemporary cemeteries of the Carpathian Basin, was a social phenomenon at that time. It may even have been a permitted act, whose motives may have arisen from complex philosophical and religious ideas about the afterlife.
